# Shared corpus: "does this source DEFINE <name> at column 0?"
# GitHub #275, acceptance criterion C5.
#
# WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
# ====================
# The same question is answered twice, in two languages, by two independent
# implementations:
#
#   * Python -- tools/gate/check_duplicate_test_definitions.py, via
#     definition_sizes(): TYPE_DEF / FUNC_DEF / NOT_A_DEF plus _opens_a_body().
#   * C++    -- tests/test_oracle_standard.cpp, definesHelperAtColumnZero().
#
# Nothing compared them. GitHub #275 is the issue filed because a ~155-line
# helper (DirectoryAttacker) was defined TWICE and the guard could not see it;
# the deeper point the issue makes is that two copies of a thing drift. That
# applies to the DETECTOR as much as to the helper it detects, and a drift here
# is worse than a drift in a helper: both sides would still look green, each
# against its own tests.
#
# So both implementations read THIS file and must agree with it. If they ever
# disagree with each other, at least one disagrees with the corpus and fails.
# The corpus is the single source of truth; neither implementation is.
#
# FORMAT
# ======
# Directives begin with '@' at column 0. A source line may NOT begin with '@'
# (both readers assert this rather than silently truncating a case).
#
#   @case   <id>          unique, kebab-case
#   @name   <symbol>      the symbol being asked about
#   @expect 1 | 0         1 = this source DEFINES <name> at column 0
#   @why    <one line>    why that is the right answer
#   @src                  source lines follow, verbatim, until @end
#   @end
#
# Lines outside a case that start with '#' are comments.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART 1 -- the seven cases #275's own C++ tests already pin.
# C5 names these explicitly. Both sides already agree on all seven (measured
# before this corpus was written); they are here so that agreement is ENFORCED
# rather than coincidental.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

@case type-definition-with-body
@name DirectoryAttacker
@expect 1
@why The shape that was invisible before #275: a TYPE, with neither a '(' nor one of the four return-type prefixes the old matcher required.
@src
struct DirectoryAttacker {
    std::atomic<bool> stop{false};
    void start() {}
};
@end

@case different-name
@name DirectoryAttacker
@expect 0
@why A differently-named struct must not match, or the detector is simply always true.
@src
struct SomethingElse {
};
@end

@case forward-declaration
@name DirectoryAttacker
@expect 0
@why Every header is entitled to a forward declaration; counting them makes the guard fire on correct code.
@src
struct DirectoryAttacker;
@end

@case indented-definition
@name DirectoryAttacker
@expect 0
@why Outside the stated scope (column 0 only). The limit is deliberate, but it must be the limit it claims rather than an accident.
@src
    struct DirectoryAttacker {
    };
@end

@case name-is-a-prefix
@name DirectoryAttacker
@expect 0
@why DirectoryAttackerHelper must not match DirectoryAttacker; a prefix match would fire on unrelated types sharing a leading substring.
@src
struct DirectoryAttackerHelper {
};
@end

@case function-non-allowlisted-return
@name seenNames
@expect 1
@why A return type outside std::string/bool/void/int. That four-prefix allowlist was the hand-made-population defect one level down, and removing it is half of what #275 asked for.
@src
std::set<std::string> seenNames(int n) {
    return {};
}
@end

@case function-declaration
@name applyProtectedDacl
@expect 0
@why A declaration is not a definition.
@src
bool applyProtectedDacl(const char* p);
@end

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART 2 -- shapes chosen to make the two sides DISAGREE if they can.
#
# Part 1 is agreement on cases both sides were already written against, which
# is the weaker half of the evidence: a corpus assembled only from a detector's
# own passing tests cannot find drift. These probe the places the two
# implementations are structurally different.
#
# multiline-function-declaration is a REAL DEFECT found by exactly this
# comparison, not a hypothetical: tests/support/SaveFailureInjection.h:312-316
# declares killChildInsideSaveWindow across five lines with the ';' four lines
# below the name. The Python side hit this on its first run, wrongly reported
# the header as a second DEFINITION, and was fixed by balancing the parameter
# list (_opens_a_body). The C++ mirror checks only the FIRST line for ';' and
# never got that fix.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

@case multiline-function-declaration
@name killChildInsideSaveWindow
@expect 0
@why The real shape at tests/support/SaveFailureInjection.h:312-316 -- the ';' is four lines below the name, so a first-line-only check reads a DECLARATION as a definition. A helper declared in a header and defined in a .cpp would then count twice and the guard would fire on correct code.
@src
KilledSaveResult killChildInsideSaveWindow(
    const std::filesystem::path& sourcePdf,
    const std::filesystem::path& target,
    const std::string& gtestFilterForVictim,
    std::chrono::milliseconds waitForWindow = std::chrono::seconds(30));
@end

@case multiline-function-definition
@name killChildInsideSaveWindow
@expect 1
@why The positive twin of the case above, and it is load-bearing: without it the fix could be "a multi-line signature is never a definition", which would blind the detector to every helper whose parameters wrap.
@src
KilledSaveResult killChildInsideSaveWindow(
    const std::filesystem::path& sourcePdf,
    int attempts)
{
    return {};
}
@end

@case body-opens-on-next-line
@name seenNames
@expect 1
@why A definition whose '{' is on the following line is still a definition; a rule keyed on '{' appearing alongside the name would miss it.
@src
std::set<std::string> seenNames(int n)
{
    return {};
}
@end

@case constructor-initialiser-list
@name DirectoryAttacker
@expect 1
@why An initialiser list opens a definition without a '{' on the signature line.
@src
DirectoryAttacker::DirectoryAttacker(int n)
    : count(n)
{
}
@end

@case multiline-type-with-base
@name DirectoryAttacker
@expect 1
@why A class whose base-clause wraps; the '{' is two lines below the name.
@src
class DirectoryAttacker
    : public Base
{
};
@end

@case enum-class-definition
@name Mode
@expect 1
@why 'enum class' is one of the type spellings the detector claims to cover.
@src
enum class Mode {
    A,
};
@end

@case enum-class-forward
@name Mode
@expect 0
@why An opaque enum declaration is not a definition.
@src
enum class Mode : int;
@end

@case name-inside-a-call-is-not-a-definition
@name DirectoryAttacker
@expect 0
@why The name appears, at column 4, inside a call. Only column-0 definitions count, and a substring search would be fooled.
@src
void use() {
    DirectoryAttacker(1);
}
@end

@case trailing-comment-after-declaration
@name applyProtectedDacl
@expect 0
@why Still a declaration; a trailing comment must not change the verdict.
@src
bool applyProtectedDacl(const char* p);  // declared here
@end

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART 3 -- the two DEFENSIVE branches of the C++ look-ahead.
#
# Added after a claim-check gate failed this phase for them. `opensABodyAfterParams`
# makes two behavioural claims in its own comment -- a 40-line bound, and
# "ran out of look-ahead -> NOT a definition" -- and the 16 cases above
# exercised neither, because every one of them resolves within a few lines. A
# described mechanism that nothing couples to the code is this project's
# recurring defect shape, and it had just been introduced by the fix for
# another instance of it.
#
# Python's `_opens_a_body` carries the same 40-line limit_hint, and was measured
# to agree with all four cases below BEFORE they were written down -- otherwise
# the corpus would have been encoding a divergence rather than pinning a shared
# behaviour.
#
# The pair matters in both directions:
#   * `signature-wraps-twenty-lines-then-body` is @expect 1, so it reddens if
#     the bound SHRINKS below ~21;
#   * `closes-beyond-the-look-ahead-bound` is @expect 0, so it reddens if the
#     bound GROWS past ~51;
#   * `parameter-list-never-closes` is @expect 0, so it reddens if the fallback
#     flips to "definition".
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

@case signature-wraps-twenty-lines-then-body
@name wrapsTwenty
@expect 1
@why A real definition whose parameter list wraps about twenty lines before the body opens. Well inside the 40-line look-ahead, so it must resolve as a definition -- this is the case that fails if the bound is ever reduced.
@src
KilledSaveResult wrapsTwenty(
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int a,
    int z)
{
    return {};
}
@end

@case parameter-list-never-closes
@name wideOpen
@expect 0
@why An unbalanced '(' -- the unclosed '#if' arm shape the bound exists for. Neither side can resolve it, and both must fall back to NOT a definition: a guard that treats an unresolvable shape as duplication fires on correct code. This is the case that fails if the fallback is ever flipped.
@src

@case closes-beyond-the-look-ahead-bound
@name farAway
@expect 0
@why HONEST LIMITATION, not a correctness claim: this IS a definition, and both implementations report it as not one, because its body opens beyond the 40-line look-ahead. Recorded so the shared limit is pinned rather than incidental -- if someone widens the bound, this case reddens and the change becomes a decision instead of a side effect.
